summary:
Yobe State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the statute reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Yobe is one of those twelve states. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the capital's police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by police in Nigeria's largest city, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office note (Version 4.0, June 2025) separates the two layers a visitor comes under. The federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment and three years for attempt, and is silent on women; the Sharia penal codes of the twelve northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment.

Enforcement is uneven in practice. The same note records few secular cases reaching court, which leaves the ban on cross-dressing and public expression to be enforced administratively rather than through prosecution; its enforcement and Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023.

The one trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion; an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
Yobe State's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, and Sharia law was established in the state in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim. Yobe adopted Sharia within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims.

Because Yobe is one of the twelve states listed by Human Rights Watch as having adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, its Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law. Muslim residents therefore face the death maximum for male same-sex acts and the flogging and imprisonment penalties for acts between women, while the federal offences remain available to secular prosecutors.

The Hisbah enforcement apparatus recorded in the UK Home Office note operates in this layer of northern states, and its documented 2023 response to public cross-dressing was corporal rather than prosecutorial.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here; no statute, commencement date or penalty is sourced.

The public floggings of persons cross-dressing recorded in the UK Home Office note for 2023 are not located to a specific state in the material reviewed, so their occurrence in Yobe itself is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence case, killing or prosecution in Yobe is documented in these sources; the killing of Abuja Area Mama and the police extortion case both occurred outside the state. Whether a trans detainee in Yobe would be housed in a male or female section is not sourced, and the Bobrisky placement question was left to official discretion.

The number of SSMPA or Sharia same-sex prosecutions actually brought in Yobe is not stated in any source reviewed here.
